title: T1566.004 — Phishing - Spearphishing Voice
subtitle: Watch the call unfold: the attacker’s preparation, the spoofed caller ID, the victim’s decisions, and what the SOC can see at the same time.
aria: Animated diagram of a spearphishing voice attack: the attacker spoofs caller ID, calls an employee posing as IT support, obtains an MFA approval and remote access tool installation, then resets authentication through the tricked help desk. A full written description of every step follows below the canvas.

nodes.label: Attacker (Voice)
nodes.tip: The threat actor on the phone. They research the target, spoof the caller ID, and run the urgency script.

nodes.label: VoIP + Spoof
nodes.tip: The attacker's telephony setup. VoIP services let any displayed caller ID be set freely, which is why the number proves nothing.

nodes.label: Employee (Phone)
nodes.tip: The person receiving the call. No software is compromised yet - the attack works through trust, urgency, and helpfulness.

nodes.label: Workstation
nodes.tip: The victim's computer. It becomes compromised when the victim installs the tool the caller requested.

nodes.label: Remote Access Tool
nodes.tip: A legitimate remote-support program (AnyDesk, TeamViewer, ScreenConnect style) installed by the victim and used by the attacker for full control.

nodes.label: IdP / Help Desk
nodes.tip: The identity provider and the human help desk. Both can be manipulated by a confident caller with good background details.

nodes.label: SOC / Defender
nodes.tip: The security operations center. It must join phone metadata, identity logs, and endpoint telemetry to see the attack at all.

steps.title: Research the target
steps.caption: the attacker gathers names, roles, and phone numbers from public sources and breach data, picks a plausible victim, and scripts the call with answers to likely objections.
steps.defender: Reduce your public footprint: trim staff lists and direct-dial numbers, and monitor what breach data exposes about your employees.

detection.label: No detection
detection.detail: This activity is not visible to the victim yet.

steps.title: Spoof the caller ID
steps.caption: through a VoIP service the attacker sets the displayed number to the company help desk line or a local number, then places the call.
steps.defender: Teach staff that caller ID is unverified data. Consider technical flags your PBX can add for calls from outside the corporate trunk.

steps.title: Run the story
steps.caption: the caller plays IT support, reports a break-in on the account, and creates urgency. The victim, trying to help, follows the caller's instructions.
steps.defender: The story always mixes authority, urgency, and a helpful reason. Train one reflex: hang up and call back on the official internal number.

fields.detail: Run the story: the caller plays IT support, reports a break-in on the account, and creates urgency.

detection.label: No detection
detection.detail: This activity is not visible to the victim yet.

steps.title: Harvest the MFA event
steps.caption: the attacker triggers a real login attempt. The victim approves the push or reads the one-time code aloud. The identity provider sees a normal successful authentication.
steps.defender: Alert on MFA approvals that follow password resets or occur at odd hours, and always verify identity out of band before reading any code to anyone.

steps.title: Install the remote tool
steps.caption: the caller sends the victim to a website and walks them through installing a support tool. The workstation now runs a remote-access program with the user's own rights.
steps.defender: User-installed remote tools are your blind spot. Application control or an EDR rule should flag first-seen remote software instantly.

detection.label: No detection
detection.detail: This activity is not visible to the victim yet.

steps.title: Take over the machine
steps.caption: the attacker connects through the remote tool, sees the screen, dumps saved credentials, and maps internal systems while the victim watches their own mouse move.
steps.defender: Remote-tool relay connections from a workstation are high-signal. Block unapproved relays at the proxy and alert on any that connect.

detection.label: Partial signal
detection.detail: A weak signal exists but is not yet a confirmed alert.

steps.title: Make the access permanent
steps.caption: the attacker enrolls a new MFA device on the compromised account, or calls the help desk and gets an MFA reset for an 'executive with a broken phone.'
steps.defender: New MFA enrollment and help desk resets are your last chance to stop account takeover. Alert immediately, and require strong verification for both.

detection.label: Alert raised
detection.detail: The SOC has enough evidence to open an incident.

steps.title: Defender responds
steps.caption: the SOC joins call metadata, identity events, and endpoint signals, isolates the host, revokes tokens and MFA factors, blocks relay domains, and hardens the help desk procedure.
steps.defender: The permanent fixes: verify reset requests out of band with a known contact, prefer phishing-resistant MFA, and allowlist remote tools by policy.
